title: Integrated Fauna of GLMZ: A Field Guide to the Ones That Got Out
body:
# Integrated Fauna of GLMZ: A Field Guide to the Ones That Got Out

## Foreword

The following species are not native to GLMZ. None of them were supposed to be here. All of them are, and have been for long enough that ecologists are beginning to stop calling them invasive and start calling them residents. This guide does not attempt to catalog all escaped specimens in the metropolitan area — that would require a volume considerably larger than this one — but focuses on those that have achieved stable breeding populations, ecological integration, or sufficient cultural visibility that a GLMZ resident might expect to encounter them.

That something was designed in a laboratory does not, it turns out, make it less capable of finding food, shelter, and suitable mates in an urban environment. In some cases it makes them considerably more capable.

---

## The Volt Rat (Mus laboratoricus illuminans)

**Escaped**: Korvax Biosystems, mid-2190s. Lab fire, mass egress.

**Current range**: All tiers of GLMZ, densest in the Gray Zone and Circuit electrical corridors.

The Volt Rat was engineered for conductive tissue research — specifically for developing bioelectric shielding materials. The result was a rat with a resting bioelectric field of approximately 2 milliamps, and the ability to discharge up to 8 milliamps when threatened. This is not enough to seriously harm a human. It is enough to make grasping one by hand memorable.

Volt Rats have established themselves in every electrical corridor, junction box room, and server closet in GLMZ. They nest in cable runs. They are attracted to electromagnetic fields. They do not eat the cables — they appear to use the fields for thermoregulation. The power grid has not been harmed. The maintenance workers who encounter them in junction boxes would dispute this characterization of harmlessness. They are small (80-100g), brown-grey, and distinguishable from common rats by the faint blue-white glow visible in their ears when they are startled.

Street status: Tolerated. Some the Gray Zone residents keep them as pets. They are called 'sparkers' in the lower tiers.

---

## The Mossglass Lizard (Chamaeleo viridis laboris)

**Escaped**: Varista Genomics, 2201. Security failure during relocation.

**Current range**: Upper tiers, building exteriors, particularly glass-faced towers in the Ledger and upper Circuit districts.

Engineered as a surface-monitoring organism — the Mossglass Lizard was designed to cling to glass surfaces and transmit thermal imaging data via implanted biosensors. The sensors stopped transmitting when the animals escaped. Everything else kept working.

Mossglass Lizards are approximately 35cm long, brilliant green, and capable of adhering to any glass or smooth composite surface in any orientation. They have established colonies on the outer faces of glass towers throughout the upper city, where they feed on the insects attracted to interior lighting. From ground level they are invisible. From eleventh-floor windows they are common, pressing themselves flat against the glass with their color-changing skin set to glass-reflection mode — visible only as a slight distortion, like a smear, until they move.

Architects hate them. Everyone else finds them harmless and occasionally beautiful. The upper-tier buildings have stopped reporting them as infestations. They do not damage the glass. They do not enter the buildings. They are simply there, watching from outside, which a number of GLMZ residents find oddly companionable.

---

## The Cartographer Fish (Cyprinus mappens)

**Escaped**: Tidal Systems Research Institute, 2198. Flooding event.

**Current range**: GLMZ's entire underground water system, including drainage channels, flood corridors, and the flooded sub-basement network of the former Port District.

The Cartographer Fish was designed to map subterranean water systems using distributed echo-location and a collective memory architecture — each fish shares positional data with the school through a low-frequency pressure-wave communication system, building a continuous real-time map of their environment stored in aggregate across hundreds of individuals.

GLMZ's underground water system is, by current estimates, mapped to 94% accuracy by the Cartographer Fish population that now lives in it. This is higher accuracy than the city's own records. Infrastructure maintenance teams have begun, informally, using the fish's behavior — where they cluster, where they scatter, how the schools move — as an early indicator of flooding risk and pipe stress. The fish do not know they are doing this. They are just fish with very good spatial memory and a strong preference for intact corridors over compromised ones.

Size: 15-25cm. Silver-blue. Distinguishable by the faint rhythmic clicking audible when a school passes in quiet conditions.

---

## The Null Crow (Corvus nullifier)

**Escaped**: Arcturus Defense Solutions internal avian program, date classified.

**Current range**: Everywhere. All of GLMZ. They got out a long time ago.

The Null Crow was designed for signals intelligence — a crow engineered to home on, and collect near-field data from, wireless communication devices. The theory was that a bird landing on a window ledge near a meeting room would be invisible. The theory was correct. The weaponized version required a retrieval mechanism that was never successfully miniaturized.

The escaped Null Crows no longer transmit data to anyone. But they still collect. They are drawn to active wireless devices. They land near them. They sit and they watch. They are considerably larger than standard crows — 60cm wingspan — and their plumage has a slight metallic sheen from the conductive thread woven into feathers for antenna function that is now purely decorative.

GLMZ residents have developed a folk belief that Null Crows are bad luck, or surveillance, or both. Technically the surveillance belief is thirty years out of date. The Null Crows are not transmitting. They are just watching. People persist in finding this uncomfortable.

Nickname throughout GLMZ: 'Listeners.' They are everywhere. They do not bother anyone. They simply pay attention in a way that feels institutional.

---

## The Substrate Mold (Fungus architectus)

**Escaped**: Vela BioConstruct, 2207. Disposal incident.

**Current range**: Structural elements of the Gray Zone and lower Circuit, particularly older reinforced concrete.

The Substrate Mold was designed as a construction material supplement — a fungal organism that would grow into and around concrete reinforcement, filling microcracks, depositing calcium carbonate compounds that increased compressive strength, essentially using biological processes to self-repair aging infrastructure. It worked. The problem was containment: once it found a crack to grow into, it did not distinguish between the structure it was supposed to repair and adjacent structures it wasn't.

the sprawl's oldest buildings, built in the 2050s and 2060s, are now extensively colonized by Substrate Mold. Structural engineers have stopped removing it because removal appears to accelerate deterioration. The mold, left alone, seems to have reached an equilibrium with the buildings: it fills cracks as they form, expands into new voids when concrete shifts, and in several documented cases has bridged failed rebar with fungal growth strong enough to maintain load-bearing function.

The mold is invisible within the concrete. Its presence is detectable only by the faint bioluminescent blue-green glow visible in deep cracks in low-light conditions — a byproduct of its metabolic process. In the oldest parts of the Gray Zone, where the buildings have been breathing with Substrate Mold for fifteen years, the walls in certain stairwells glow faintly in the dark. Residents have learned to find this comforting rather than alarming. The glow means the building is alive, in the sense that matters.

---

## A Note on the Others

This guide covers five species. The full inventory of escaped laboratory organisms living in GLMZ is unknown. Estimates range from forty-two to several hundred. Most are benign or, like the Substrate Mold, have become functionally integrated into the urban ecosystem. Some are not. The GLMZ Environmental Management Authority maintains a register of confirmed escaped specimens and accepts reports, though their resources for field investigation are limited.

The city does not publicize the register.
